    Document Processing and XML Extraction

    document-processing-extraction.Rmd

    Introduction

    This page details the first step of working with CheckrefR: turning a document or a list of references into usable data. The “Get started” page gave an overview; here we go into how each function works.

    We will cover, in turn:

    1. grobid_process_file(): the central function, which sends one document to GROBID and retrieves the result. We will present the four available services, their parameters, and the two output “paths” (raw XML or data table), as well as the parse_*() functions that turn the XML into a table.
    2. grobid_process_files(): a function that repeats the processing on several documents, with parallel execution and error handling.
    3. process_citation_file(): a shortcut for processing a text file containing a list of references.
    4. parse_apa_text(): an alternative without GROBID, which extracts reference information in APA 7 format using regular expressions.

    These four functions perform related tasks: producing, from different sources, structured references (title, authors, year, DOI…) ready for validation.

    Reminder: GROBID and XML. GROBID is a tool that reads a document (PDF) or a free-text reference and extracts the bibliographic information from it. It returns its result in a format called TEI/XML, a tagged text file that is machine-readable but not very convenient for analysis. CheckrefR can therefore give you this XML as is (“raw”), or convert it into a data table (“parsed”).

    grobid_process_file(): processing a document

    Principle

    grobid_process_file() sends a single file to GROBID, locally or remotely, and returns the result. It takes care of checking that the server is running for you (see “Get started” and the server administration page).

    grobid_process_file(
  file,
  service       = "processFulltextDocument",
  params        = list(),
  output_dir    = NULL,
  output_format = "parsed",
  mode          = NULL,
  model_type    = .checkrefr_env$grobid_model_type,
  verbose       = TRUE,
  user_agent    = NULL
)

    The arguments fall into three groups:

    Group Arguments Role
    What to process file, service, params The document, the type of analysis requested, the GROBID options
    What to get output_format, output_dir Format of the result, optional saving of the XML
    Where and how mode, model_type, verbose, user_agent Server used and technical behavior

    Choosing a service

    The service argument indicates which type of analysis GROBID should perform. There are four services:

    service Expected input What you get Associated parsing function
    "processFulltextDocument" (default) a PDF The full text, split into sections parse_fulltext()
    "processHeaderDocument" a PDF The header metadata (title, authors, abstract, DOI…) parse_header()
    "processReferences" a PDF The list of references cited in the document parse_references()
    "processCitationList" a .txt file or a vector of references Structured references from free text parse_citation_list()

    Which service should you choose? To validate the references of an article, the processReferences service is generally the most direct: it returns only the bibliography. Use processFulltextDocument if you also need the text of the article, processHeaderDocument if you are only interested in the article’s metadata, and processCitationList if your references are already in a text file (one per line).

    The first three services require a PDF. Only processCitationList accepts a .txt text file or directly a vector of references.

    The two output paths: output_format

    The output_format argument determines what the function returns to you. It accepts two values:

    output_format Result When to use it
    "parsed" (default) A data table (tibble), ready for analysis Common case: you want to work with the data in R
    "raw" The raw XML (a character string) You want to keep or inspect GROBID’s exact response

    output_format = "parsed" path: a directly usable table

    With the default value, CheckrefR automatically converts the XML into a table, using the parsing function corresponding to the chosen service. A source_file column is added: it contains the name of the processed file.

    refs <- grobid_process_file(
  file    = "mon_article.pdf",
  service = "processReferences"
)

head(refs)

    output_format = "raw" path: raw XML and the parse_*() functions

    With "raw", you get the XML as GROBID produced it, in the form of a character string. This lets you keep it, inspect it, or convert it yourself later.

    xml <- grobid_process_file(
  file          = "mon_article.pdf",
  service       = "processReferences",
  output_format = "raw"
)

substr(xml, 1, 300)   # preview of the beginning of the XML

    The conversion into a table is handled by four public functions, one per service. They are called automatically in the "parsed" path, but you can also use them directly on XML you already have:

    Function Associated service Content of the returned table
    parse_fulltext() processFulltextDocument One row per section (title, abstract, body, acknowledgements, appendices), with the text (content), the word count (n_words) and paragraph count (n_paragraphs)
    parse_header() processHeaderDocument A single row: title, authors, journal, year, DOI, abstract, keywords, language, number of references (n_references)
    parse_references() processReferences One row per reference: raw reference, title, authors, year, journal, volume, pages, DOI…
    parse_citation_list() processCitationList One row per parsed reference, with a confidence indicator (parse_confidence) and a reference type (ref_type) 
    # The same XML can be converted with the appropriate function
refs   <- parse_references(xml)
header <- parse_header(xml)
texte  <- parse_fulltext(xml)

    One parse_*() function per service. The XML returned by each service has a different structure. You must therefore use the parse_*() function that matches the service with which the XML was obtained. These functions accept XML as text, as a file, or as an xml2 object.

    Saving the XML with output_dir

    The output_dir argument lets you write the XML to disk, in a folder that is created if necessary. The file is named after the source document, followed by the .tei.xml extension (for a list of references sent as a vector, it is called citations.tei.xml).

    grobid_process_file(
  file       = "mon_article.pdf",
  service    = "processReferences",
  output_dir = "xml_sortie"
)

    Points to note about output_dir.

    • When output_dir is specified, the function returns the raw XML (invisibly), and not the path of the written file, regardless of the value of output_format.
    • There is no protection against overwriting: if a file with the same name already exists in the folder, it is replaced without warning.

    Tuning the analysis with params

    The params argument is a list of options passed as is to GROBID. They let you adjust the processing: for example, asking GROBID to consolidate the references by checking them against an external database, or to keep the raw text of the references.

    refs <- grobid_process_file(
  file    = "mon_article.pdf",
  service = "processReferences",
  params  = list(consolidateCitations = 1)
)

    The available parameters depend on the service and the GROBID version. The most common ones are:

    Parameter Effect (briefly) Services concerned
    consolidateHeader Consolidates the header metadata with an external database Header, full text
    consolidateCitations Consolidates the references with an external database References, full text, citation list
    includeRawCitations Includes the raw text of the references in the XML References, citation list
    segmentSentences Splits the text into sentences Full text
    teiCoordinates Adds the coordinates of the elements in the PDF Full text, references

    For the complete list, the possible values and their exact effect, see the GROBID API documentation.

    Good to know.

    • No validation is performed on params: CheckrefR passes your options to GROBID without checking them. An unknown or misspelled option will simply be ignored or rejected by GROBID.
    • includeRawCitations is added automatically (value 1) for the processReferences and processCitationList services, so that the original reference is kept in the raw_reference column.
    • Consolidation (consolidateHeader, consolidateCitations) relies on external services: it slows down processing and may alter the returned metadata. If your goal is to verify references with validate_references(), it is generally preferable not to consolidate beforehand, so as not to “correct” upstream the errors you are trying to detect.

    Server, model, and other arguments

    The mode ("docker" or "remote") and model_type ("crf" or "full") arguments determine which GROBID server is used and which model it applies. They were presented in “Get started” and are detailed in the “GROBID Server Setup and Administration” page: we do not return to them here. Simply remember that, if the server is not running, it is started or reached automatically.

    The other arguments are more technical in use:

    Argument Role
    verbose Displays (TRUE) or hides progress messages
    .ensure_server If TRUE (default), checks or starts the server before the request. Set to FALSE only if you manage the server yourself
    user_agent Identification text sent to the server. By default, CheckrefR identifies itself with its name and version

    Behavior when something goes wrong

    • If the server is temporarily overloaded (HTTP 503 response, common on demonstration servers), the request is automatically retried, up to 3 times, with a 10-second wait between attempts.
    • If GROBID returns no result, the function returns NA (invisibly).
    • A missing file or one of the wrong type (for example a .txt for a PDF service) triggers an explicit error.

    grobid_process_files(): processing several documents

    Principle

    grobid_process_files() applies grobid_process_file() to each element of a vector of paths. It therefore reuses the same service, params, output_dir, output_format, mode, model_type and user_agent arguments, with the same meaning. It adds what is needed to process a batch: parallelism, progress bar, error handling and result assembly.

    grobid_process_files(
  files,
  service       = "processFulltextDocument",
  params        = list(),
  output_dir    = NULL,
  output_format = "parsed",
  parallel      = length(files) > 5L,
  n_workers     = .checkrefr_env $ max_workers,
  progress      = TRUE,
  mode          = NULL,
  model_type    = .checkrefr_env $ grobid_model_type,
  on_error      = "warn",
  user_agent    = NULL
)
    pdfs <- list.files("mes_pdf", pattern = "\\.pdf$", full.names = TRUE)

refs <- grobid_process_files(
  files   = pdfs,
  service = "processReferences"
)

    The function does not scan a folder. files must be a vector of paths that has already been built (for example with list.files()). There is no argument to filter by pattern, traverse subfolders or skip files that have already been processed.

    The added arguments

    Argument Default value Role
    files (required) Vector of file paths
    parallel TRUE if more than 5 files Processes several files at the same time
    n_workers package internal value Number of simultaneous processes
    progress TRUE Displays a progress bar
    on_error "warn" What to do if a file fails: "warn" or "stop"

    Parallel processing

    Processing several files simultaneously speeds up the work. The number of simultaneous processes depends on the mode:

    • "docker" mode: the requested number (n_workers) is capped at the number of cores on your computer minus one.
    • "remote" mode: the number is always set to 2, regardless of the requested value, so as not to overload the demonstration servers.

    Progress bar. The progress argument only has an effect in sequential processing (without parallelism). In parallel mode, no bar is displayed.

    Error handling: on_error

    • on_error = "warn" (default): if a file fails, a warning is issued and processing continues with the following files. The file concerned yields an NA result.
    • on_error = "stop": processing stops at the first error.

    For a large batch, the default value is generally the most practical: a faulty file does not block the whole run.

    What the function returns

    The result depends on output_dir and output_format:

    Situation Result
    output_format = "parsed", without output_dir A single table combining the results of all files (source_file column to tell them apart). Files that failed are absent from it. If no file succeeded, the function returns NULL.
    output_format = "raw", without output_dir A list of raw XML, named after the files. Files that failed appear in it with the value NA.
    With output_dir The XML files are written to the folder; the function returns, invisibly, a vector of raw XML (and not of paths). 
    # Get a list of raw XML, one per file
xmls <- grobid_process_files(
  files         = pdfs,
  service       = "processReferences",
  output_format = "raw"
)

names(xmls)   # names of the processed files

    process_citation_file(): processing a file of references

    Principle

    process_citation_file() is a shortcut for the case where your references are already in a text file (one reference per line). It does three things:

    1. reads the file and ignores empty lines;
    2. calls grobid_process_file() with the processCitationList service;
    3. returns either the XML or the table of parsed references.

    It is equivalent to calling grobid_process_file() with service = "processCitationList", but only requires the file.

    process_citation_file(
  file,
  params        = list(),
  output_format = "parsed",
  model_type    = .checkrefr_env$grobid_model_type,
  verbose       = TRUE
)

    Example with ref_test.txt 

    chemin_ref <- system.file("extdata", "ref_test.txt", package = "CheckrefR")

refs_grobid <- process_citation_file(chemin_ref)

refs_grobid |>
  select(ref_n, title, year, doi, parse_confidence) |>
  head(6)

    The returned table contains one row per recognized reference, with in particular:

    Column Content
    ref_n Reference number
    raw_reference Original text of the line
    title, authors, authors_list, year Extracted metadata
    journal, publisher, volume, issue, pages Publication information
    doi, pmid, url Identifiers
    ref_type Inferred document type
    parse_confidence GROBID’s confidence score for the parsing

    Limits of this shortcut. process_citation_file() does not offer a choice of mode (local or remote), nor output_dir, nor user_agent: it uses the package’s active configuration. If you need these settings, call grobid_process_file() directly with service = "processCitationList". Moreover, the match between the original text and each reference is made by position: if GROBID recognizes a different number of references than the number of lines, a warning indicates that some raw_reference values will be NA.

    parse_apa_text(): extracting without GROBID

    Principle

    parse_apa_text() performs the same task as process_citation_file() (turning free-text references into structured data), but without GROBID: it relies on regular expressions, that is, text patterns, adapted to the APA 7 format. It therefore works offline and instantly, but only for well-formed references in this format.

    parse_apa_text(
  input,
  as_ref_df         = FALSE,
  source_file_label = "APA_Input"
)

    The input argument accepts three types of input: a vector of references, the path to a .txt file, or a single-column table.

    Example with ref_test.txt 

    chemin_ref <- system.file("extdata", "ref_test.txt", package = "CheckrefR")

apa <- parse_apa_text(chemin_ref)

apa |>
  select(title, doi, publication_year, authorships) |>
  head(6) |>
  kable_site(caption = "References extracted by parse_apa_text()")
    References extracted by parse_apa_text()
    title doi publication_year authorships
    The “what” and “why” of goal pursuits: Human needs and the self-determination of behavior 10.1207/s15327965pli1104_01 2000 Deci, E; Ryan, R
    Efficient estimation of word representations in vector space NA 2013 Mikolov, T; Chen, K; Corrado, G; Dean, J
    Attention is all you need 10.48550/arxiv.1706.03762 2017 Vaswani, A; Shazeer, N; Parmar, N; Uszkoreit, J; Jones, L; Gomez, A; Kaiser, Ł; Polosukhin, I
    Thinking, fast and slow NA 2011 Kahneman, D
    The need to belong: Desire for interpersonal attachments as a fundamental human motivation NA 1995 Baumeister, R; Leary, M
    Self-efficacy: Toward a unifying theory of behavioral change 10.1037/0003-066x.55.1.5 1977 Bandura, A

    Two output formats: as_ref_df

    as_ref_df Columns returned Use
    FALSE (default) raw_reference, title, doi, publication_year, authorships, authorships_list Inspect what the extraction recognized
    TRUE raw_reference, source_file, ref_n, title, doi, year, authors, authors_list Format ready for validate_references()

    With as_ref_df = TRUE, the function applies format_apa_for_validation(), which renames and completes the columns (reference number, source name given by source_file_label). The output can then be passed directly to validation.

    refs_apa <- parse_apa_text(chemin_ref, as_ref_df = TRUE)

refs_apa |>
  select(ref_n, title, year, doi) |>
  head(6) |>
  kable_site(caption = "Format ready for validation (as_ref_df = TRUE)")
    Format ready for validation (as_ref_df = TRUE)
    ref_n title year doi
    1 The “what” and “why” of goal pursuits: Human needs and the self-determination of behavior 2000 10.1207/s15327965pli1104_01
    2 Efficient estimation of word representations in vector space 2013 NA
    3 Attention is all you need 2017 10.48550/arxiv.1706.03762
    4 Thinking, fast and slow 2011 NA
    5 The need to belong: Desire for interpersonal attachments as a fundamental human motivation 1995 NA
    6 Self-efficacy: Toward a unifying theory of behavioral change 1977 10.1037/0003-066x.55.1.5

    How the function reads a reference

    The function identifies the following elements, in this order:

    Element Rule applied
    DOI A https://doi.org/... link at the end of the reference
    Year The first year in parentheses, for example (2020) or (2020a)
    Title The text following the year, up to the first period
    Authors Surname, Initials patterns located before the year (separated by commas or &)

    Limits of regular-expression extraction.

    • DOI: only a DOI written as a complete link at the end of the reference is recognized. A DOI written differently (doi:10...) or placed elsewhere is ignored.
    • Title: the end of the title is detected at the first period. A title containing a period (abbreviation, number) will be truncated.
    • Authors: only the Surname, Initials forms are recognized, with an abbreviated first name. A full first name or an unusual order may not be recognized.
    • Format: the function assumes correctly formed APA 7 references. Poorly formatted references, or those produced in another style, will yield missing or incorrect fields.

    These limits make it a fast but strict tool: for heterogeneous or imperfect references, process_citation_file() (via GROBID) is generally more tolerant.

    Choosing the right function

    Your situation Recommended function
    One PDF, you want its references grobid_process_file() with service = "processReferences"
    One PDF, you want its text and sections grobid_process_file() with service = "processFulltextDocument"
    One PDF, you want its metadata grobid_process_file() with service = "processHeaderDocument"
    Several PDFs grobid_process_files()
    A text file of references (varied formats) process_citation_file()
    A text file of references in APA 7, without a server parse_apa_text()
    XML already obtained, to be converted parse_fulltext(), parse_header(), parse_references() or parse_citation_list()

    Whichever path you choose, the “parsed” output or parse_apa_text(as_ref_df = TRUE) can be passed to validate_references(), presented in the “Reference Validation Pipeline and Scoring” page.
